claims.text: The strength and deformation or failure behavior of multi-component concentrated alloys is governed by interactions between dislocations and grain boundaries.
Dislocation and grain-boundary interactions can be modeled using molecular dynamics simulations.
Temperature, strain rate, and loading mode are relevant parameters for simulations of dislocation dynamics and grain-boundary interactions.
The proposed tests span temperatures of 300 K, 500 K, and 700 K.
The proposed tests span strain rates of 10^-3, 10^-2, and 10^-1 s^-1.
The proposed loading modes include uniaxial tension, compression, and shear.
Dislocation density and grain-boundary character are the structural mediators governing mechanical behavior.
The governing mechanisms are dislocation glide, dislocation–grain-boundary interactions, and grain-boundary sliding.
The target multi-component concentrated alloy will have 20% higher yield strength than a simpler-composition baseline alloy.
The target multi-component concentrated alloy will have 30% lower ductility than a simpler-composition baseline alloy.
Yield strength and ductility will be measured by uniaxial tensile testing.
Al0.5CoCrFeNi is proposed as an example of a simpler-composition baseline alloy.
The hypothesis should hold when all major-element concentrations exceed 5 at.%.
The hypothesis should hold for grain sizes between 1 and 10 micrometers.
Simulation accuracy and transferability to real alloys may limit the hypothesis.
Precipitates and pores may affect the observed mechanical behavior independently of the proposed mediators.
A correlation coefficient below 0.5 between mechanical properties and the predicted dislocation density and grain-boundary character would falsify the hypothesis.
